summary: Desert Hot Springs sits on a geological oddity: the Mission Creek Fault runs directly beneath the city, and the same tectonic activity that makes the Coachella Valley seismically active also pushes naturally heated mineral water to the surface on one side of the fault and cold aquifer water on the other — all within the same small city. That geothermal quirk has fueled a cluster of small spa and wellness operations that form a real, if modest, piece of the local economy alongside healthcare and service-sector jobs. At a median home value of $309,300 against a median household income of $50,349, the price-to-income ratio lands around 6.1 — genuinely cheaper than most of Southern California but still a stretch at that income level, where a conventional mortgage payment would consume a painful share of gross pay. The 30.5-square-mile footprint at just 1,090 people per square mile means the city is physically sprawling and car-dependent, with subdivisions spread across alluvial fan terrain that slopes up toward the Little San Bernardino Mountains and Joshua Tree National Park's western entrance only minutes north. Summer highs regularly exceed 100°F, and that 81°F annual average daytime temperature means air conditioning isn't optional — it's a utility bill that shapes household budgets. The property crime rate of 1,428 per 100K, with motor vehicle theft notably elevated at 550, is worth weighing against those lower housing costs. Desert Hot Springs is, at its core, a place where affordable Coachella Valley real estate and proximity to genuine wilderness coexist with the infrastructural thinness of a small desert city still building out its economic base.
